1.pericope_label: Ahaz begins to reign, walks in the way of the kings of Israel, passes his son through the fire and sacrifices in the high places

schools.summary: Clarke takes the chronology head on: Ahaz was twenty at his accession and reigned sixteen years, so he died at thirty-six, yet Hezekiah was twenty-five when he succeeded, which makes Ahaz a father at eleven. He reports the proposed rendering that Ahaz was twenty when his father began to reign, which would make him fifty-two at death and twenty-seven at Hezekiah’s birth, but calls it a violent solution worthy of little credit, preferring to return to the text as it stands and allow the early marriage, since the young of both sexes in eastern countries are marriageable at ten or twelve and frequently betrothed at nine; he adds a woman of his own acquaintance who had the second of her children at fourteen. On the passing through the fire he refers the subject to his notes on Leviticus. Wesley states the rite flatly, that the passing was by way of oblation, so as to be consumed for a burnt-offering, which was the practice of the heathen and of some Israelites in imitation of them.

Keil and Delitzsch set the reign in a development rather than an incident: under the vigorous reigns of Uzziah and Jotham the earthly prosperity of the kingdom had been studiously advanced, and with the increase of wealth there had come, as the early chapters of Isaiah show, a prevalence of luxury and self-security, unrighteousness and forgetfulness of God among the upper classes; under Ahaz these sins grew into open apostasy, image-worship and idolatrous practices of every kind, until he shut up the doors of the porch of the temple and suspended the worship prescribed by the law altogether, and the punishment followed without delay. They note that the way of the kings of Israel means primarily the worship of Jehovah under the image of a calf, but that the same formula elsewhere includes the worship of Baal, which the parallel in Chronicles makes explicit. Ellicott prefers to mend the number, holding that it should probably be twenty-five with the Greek, Syriac and Arabic of the Chronicles parallel, since otherwise Ahaz was begotten when his father was ten or eleven, a thing perhaps not impossible in the East where both sexes reach maturity earlier than among Western races. On the fire he holds that the chronicler rightly explains the rite as a sacrifice by fire and that so appalling a thing is really intended, suggesting with Movers that the phrase may have originated in the idea that the burning was a kind of passage to union with the deity once the dross of the flesh had been purged away, or may be a mere euphemism; he reckons Ahaz the first Israelite king to offer such a sacrifice, no doubt as a last desperate resource against the oppression of his northern enemies, calls it absurd to suppose with Thenius that the king intended it in love to his child, and identifies the heathen in question as more particularly the Ammonites. On the places of worship he distinguishes the high places from the hills, two different prepositions being used in the Hebrew as in the English, explains that a high place was a local sanctuary and that the word could stretch to a sacred pillar or altar, and reports from Thenius that the green tree is not so much a green as a thick-foliaged and shadow-yielding one, quoting the prophet on those who burn incense under oaks and poplars because the shadow thereof is good.

Henry reads the reign as degeneracy from an inherited standing. Few and evil were his days, few because he died at thirty-six, evil because he had none of that concern and affection for the instituted service and worship of God for which David was celebrated; and since it was his honour to be of the house and lineage of David, and owing to God’s ancient covenant with David that he was on the throne at all, his wickedness was the more aggravated, for a good extraction is a disgrace to him who degenerates from it. He presses the folly of the idolatry: Ahaz was joined in no affinity with the kings of Israel, as Jehoram and Ahaziah were with the house of Ahab, but walked in their way unprompted, and where they could plead policy and reasons of state for their calf-worship he had no such pretence, so that in him it was the most unreasonable impolitic thing that could be, since they were his enemies and had proved enemies to themselves by it. On the children he allows a gradation, that he burnt some of them as Chronicles says expressly, and perhaps made others pass between two fires or be drawn through a flame in token of their dedication to the idol, Hezekiah himself not excepted though he was afterwards never the worse for it. On the high places he turns the blame back a generation, since had Jotham had zeal enough to take them away the debauching of his sons might have been prevented, those who connive at sin not knowing what dangerous snares they lay for those who come after them; and he reads the son’s preference as taste rather than conviction, Ahaz weary of the place where in his father’s time he had often been detained before the Lord and choosing hills for the better prospect and green trees for the pleasanter shade, a religion little worth which was guided by fancy and not by faith.

Gill works the chronology from the regnal years, that Jotham began in the second of Pekah and reigned sixteen years, so that his last year fell towards the end of Pekah’s seventeenth, and notes that Ahaz reigned the same number of years as his father. On the calf-worship he observes that it ran contrary to the religious sentiments in which Ahaz had been educated and against his political interest, which was the only or at least the principal thing that had swayed the kings of Israel to continue that idolatry. On the high places he marks the innovation, that none of the kings of Judah before him ever sacrificed there, for though his predecessors connived at the practice in the people they never encouraged it by their own example; and he thinks Ahaz very probably offered sacrifices there to idols, whereas the people had sacrificed to the true God, if at a wrong place.

debates.question: How is the chronology to be saved, given that Hezekiah succeeded at twenty-five?

positions.view: Keep the text and allow that Ahaz fathered him at eleven or twelve, which eastern custom makes possible; the alternative rendering is a violent solution
Emend the number to twenty-five with the Greek, Syriac and Arabic of the Chronicles parallel
Works the regnal years out from Pekah’s reign without raising the difficulty

debates.question: Was the son actually burnt, or only passed between fires?

positions.view: Actually burnt: the chronicler rightly explains it as a sacrifice by fire, and so appalling a rite is really intended
Actually burnt: the passing was by way of oblation, to be consumed for a burnt-offering
Some were burnt, but others perhaps only made to pass between two fires in token of dedication

debates.question: Why did Ahaz adopt the idolatry of the kings of Israel?

positions.view: Unprompted and against all policy, since they were his enemies and he had no affinity with them
Against both his education and his political interest, the one thing that had swayed those kings
It was the open apostasy into which the luxury and self-security of the previous reigns had grown

outliers.claim: Alone in distinguishing the high places from the hills by the Hebrew prepositions, and in reporting Movers on the burning as a supposed passage to union with the deity.
Alone in laying the high places at Jotham’s door, and alone in allowing that some of the sons may only have been passed between fires.
Alone in defending the received chronology by eastern marriage custom, with a case from his own acquaintance.

5.pericope_label: Rezin and Pekah besiege Jerusalem and fail, Elath is lost, and Ahaz buys the help of Tiglath-pileser with the temple treasure

schools.summary: Ellicott notes that the verse agrees almost word for word with the opening of the prophecy in Isaiah, and that the time is soon after the accession, Jotham having died at a critical moment while Pekah and Rezin were maturing their plans; the allies wanted to compel Judah to join them in throwing off the Assyrian yoke imposed some years before, and judged the surest way to be the dethroning of the dynasty of David for a creature of their own, the son of Tabeal. The words rendered could not overcome him are literally that they were not able to war, the allies proving unable to storm a city which Uzziah and Jotham had strongly fortified. On Elath he sets out the textual case for Edom: the words for Syria and Edom, Syrians and Edomites, are much alike in Hebrew writing, and the Hebrew margin, many manuscripts, the Greek and the Vulgate all read Edomites here, so that many critics would restore Edom throughout and take the sense to be that Rezin emancipated the Edomites from the yoke Uzziah had laid on them in order to win their active co-operation; the ordinary text is preferred by others, on which Rezin simply expelled the Jews and established a commercial colony of Syrians. He reads the verse itself as a parenthesis, the phrase at that time dating the war as the epoch when Judah lost its only harbour and chief emporium. On the tribute he turns to the monuments, where Damascus stands a two years’ siege, the earlier expedition is directed against Pekah, who probably saved himself by an instant submission, and Assyria turns on Rezin only once the northern kingdom has been settled and Damascus isolated; an inscription of the king’s seventeenth year lists tribute from Jahuhazi of Judah, that is Ahaz, which dates his submission, and a tablet since lost recorded the slaying of Rezin. On Kir he reports the usual identification with the district by the river Cyrus only to reject it, since Delitzsch objects that the one name cannot be equivalent to the other and the Assyrian empire never extended to that river, so that Kir must be considered a part of Mesopotamia. Keil and Delitzsch state the embassy plainly, that in this distress Ahaz turned to Tiglath-pileser without regarding either the word of Isaiah which promised him salvation or the prophet’s warning against an alliance with Assyria, and purchased his assistance with the gold and silver found in the treasures of the temple and palace; they place it probably after the first great victory gained by the foe. On Kir they take the opposite view, that it is a district by the river Kur, which rises in Armenia, unites with the Araxes and flows into the Caspian, allowing that the length of the river makes it impossible to define the locality precisely, and dismissing as indefinite and hardly drawn from early historical sources the statement of Josephus that the Damascenes were transported to upper Media.

Henry gives the attempt and the expedient in order. The confederates thought to make themselves masters of Jerusalem and to set a king of their own in it, and in this fell short, though the king of Syria recovered Elath, a considerable port upon the Red Sea — and Henry draws the moral that what can those keep who have lost their religion, who may expect to be always on the losing hand. On the embassy his judgment is severe: having forsaken God, Ahaz had neither courage nor strength to make head against his enemies, nor could he with any boldness ask help of God, for those whose hearts condemn them will go anywhere in a day of distress rather than to God. Was it because there was not a God in Israel that he sent to the Assyrian for help? Was the rock of ages removed out of its place, that he stayed himself on this broken reed? The sin was its own punishment, for though he gained his point he made a bad bargain: he enslaved himself in the words I am thy servant and thy son, as dutiful and obedient as to a master or father, when had he humbled himself so to God he might have been delivered upon easier terms, might have saved his money and needed only to part with his sins; and he impoverished himself besides, both church and state being squeezed and exhausted to gratify his new patron, for it is common for those who have brought themselves into straits by one sin to help themselves out by another.

Wesley credits the failure of the siege to God, who of his own mere grace undertook Ahaz’s protection and disappointed the hopes of his enemies; on the embassy he repeats Henry’s argument in brief, asking whether it was because there was no God in Israel that he sent to the Assyrian, and concluding that the sin was its own punishment, since though it served his present turn he made an ill bargain, impoverishing himself and enslaving both himself and his people. Clarke places here the sending of Isaiah to console the king, with its prediction that both Rezin and Pekah would die, and renders the submission plainly as an undertaking to obey in all and become tributary if only he were helped against Syria and Israel. He weighs the help by the parallel, which says that this king distressed Ahaz and strengthened him not: he took Damascus and slew Rezin, but gave no help against the Philistines and lent no forces against Israel, and distressed him by taking the royal and the temple treasures, so that he helped him a little but distressed him on the whole, little service for so great a sacrifice. He adds from Chronicles the scale of Pekah’s earlier success and the sending back of the captives at the prophet’s word.

Gill makes God the mover of the attack itself, the two kings coming up moved to it by the Lord to chastise Ahaz for his idolatry. On Elath he traces the port’s history, that it formerly belonged to Edom, was taken from them by David, retaken when they revolted in Joram’s time and perhaps taken again by Amaziah, since his son rebuilt it and restored it to Judah, and that by this verse it had been in Syrian hands; and he refuses the emendation outright, noting that it would mean substituting Edom for Aram, which Le Clerc has ventured to do without any authority. He observes that the silver and gold sent away were what Uzziah and Jotham had put in the house of the Lord, all that was there in the days of Amaziah having been carried off by the king of Israel.

God of his own mere grace undertook his protection and disappointed his enemies

10.pericope_label: Ahaz sees an altar at Damascus, Urijah builds its copy, the king sacrifices on it and the brasen altar is displaced

schools.summary: Ellicott holds the king’s interest artistic rather than religious, the terms for fashion and pattern and workmanship indicating as much, and quotes Robertson Smith on a character so little capable of appreciating the dangers of his new obligations that he came home with his head full of the artistic and religious curiosities of his journey, finding no more pressing concern in a national crisis than a new altar on a Damascus pattern — the work of a trifling and superstitious virtuoso who imagined that a few foreign novelties gave lustre to a reign which had fooled away the independence of Judah. He takes the great king to have held his court at Damascus after its capture and summoned the vassal princes of Palestine thither to do him homage in person, and identifies Urijah as the high priest who appears to be the credible witness of the prophecy, his high official position securing his credit as a witness. On the sacrifice he stands apart: from the present narrative it does not appear but that Ahaz offered to Jehovah, the account in Chronicles must be understood of other sacrifices instituted by him, and like most of his contemporaries he thought the traditional worship of Jehovah not incompatible with the cult of foreign deities; the verse describes a thank-offering for his late deliverance from deadly peril. He notes that every version but the Targum reads that the king went up upon the altar, so that Ahaz, like Uzziah, personally exercised the priestly function of sacrifice. On the removal he explains that the brasen altar used to stand before the Lord in the middle of the court of the priests and in front of the temple proper, that the verse seems to imply Urijah had pushed it forward nearer the sanctuary and set the new Syrian altar in its place, and that Ahaz, not satisfied with an arrangement which appeared to confer a kind of precedence on the old altar, drew it back and fixed it on the north side of his own. On the words reserving the brasen altar he canvasses the readings — for consulting God, with Rashi; a thing about which the king would think, with others; perhaps simply something for him to look at, an ornamental duplicate of the other — and rejects two conjectures, one transposing the verb’s last letters to give to draw near, which does not suit the context, and one reading to seek after the Syriac, as if the old altar of sacrifice were henceforth to be an altar of prayer. Keil and Delitzsch report from Thenius that Ahaz may have gone partly to prevent a visit from Tiglath-pileser to himself, which would not have been very welcome, defend the unusual spelling of the city’s name as one of several words in this chapter formed with the dull Syriac vowel, and give the sense of the reserving words as a thing about which he would consider. They describe the displacement precisely, the copper altar of burnt-offering removed from the front of the temple-house, from the spot between the new altar and the house of Jehovah, and placed at the north side of the new one; and they note that the new altar is called the great altar probably because it was somewhat larger than Solomon’s.

Clarke will not have the altar read as an artistic whim: it was some idolatrous altar whose shape and workmanship pleased Ahaz so well that he determined to have one like it at Jerusalem, for which he had no divine authority, and the compliance of Urijah was both mean and sinful; that he did it for an idolatrous purpose is evident from the parallel, where he sacrificed to the gods of Damascus, saying that because the gods of the kings of Syria helped them he would sacrifice to them that they might help him, and made high places to burn incense to other gods in every city of Judah. He reads every alteration specified in the chapter as made in contempt of the true God, Ahaz seeming to have intended to conform everything in the Lord’s house as nearly as possible to the idolatrous temples he had seen and to model the divine worship the same way, thus provoking to anger the Lord God of his fathers. Wesley is equally blunt on the sacrifice, that it was offered not to God but to the Syrian idols to whom that altar was appropriated, though he allows that Ahaz may not yet have utterly forsaken God but worshipped idols along with him, and that whatever was offered to the true God, in the king’s name or on the people’s behalf, was now to be offered on the new altar. On the reserved altar he follows Henry, understanding a use kept for the king, who might seek God or enquire his will by sacrifices joined with prayer when he saw fit, and repeating that having thrust it out from the use for which it was instituted he pretends to advance it above its institution, which it is common for superstitious people to do — adding that to overdo is to underdo, and that our wisdom is to do just what God has commanded.

Henry calls the substitution a bolder stroke than the worst of the kings had yet given to religion, God’s altar having hitherto continued in its place and in use. He supposes Ahaz saw the altar either while viewing the rarities of the place or rather while joining in their devotions, for when he was there he thought it no harm to do as they did; it pleased his fancy extremely, being not such a plain old-fashioned one as he had been trained up to attend at Jerusalem but curiously carved and adorned with image-work, so that Solomon had but a dull fancy compared with the ingenious artist who made this — and the pattern God showed Moses in the mount was not comparable, in his eyes, to the pattern sent from Damascus, the hearts of idolaters walking after their eyes where true worshippers worship by faith. Against Urijah he brings a formal charge: without dispute or objection he put the work in hand, perhaps as fond of it as the king or desirous to curry favour, and though he might plead that obliging the king would keep him to the temple and prevent his deserting it for the high places, he prostituted his authority and profaned the crown of his priesthood by making himself a servant to the lusts of men, and betrayed the trust that bound him to maintain God’s institutions and oppose all innovations. Had he only connived at it, or been frightened into it, or endeavoured to dissuade the king, or merely delayed until he could speak with him, it would not have been so bad. Henry holds the sacrifices were offered not to the God of Israel but to the gods of Damascus, and that when he borrowed the Syrians’ altar it was no marvel he borrowed their gods, where Naaman by contrast embraced the God of Israel on getting earth from the land of Israel to make an altar of. He marks the progress of the encroachment, that Urijah was modest enough to set the new altar at the lower end of the court and leave God’s in place, but Ahaz removed God’s to an obscure corner and put his own before the sanctuary, so that the superstitious invention at first jostled with the sacred institution and at length jostled it out — for those will soon come to make nothing of God who will not be content to make him their all. On the reserving words he takes the altar for an oracle it was never designed to be, notes the common habit of seemingly magnifying what has been thrust from its use, reports the alternative that Ahaz meant only to consider what to do with it, and relays the Jewish tradition that its brass afterwards became his famous dial; and he closes on the priest, that miserable is the case of great men when those who should reprove them for their sins strengthen and serve them in their sins.

Gill gives the distance, Damascus being a hundred and sixty miles from Jerusalem according to Bunting, and has Ahaz go when he heard the city was taken, to congratulate the victor and thank him for his assistance. On Urijah he is brief and severe: he built exactly according to the size, form, figure and carved work sent him, expressly contrary to the command of God which had fixed both the form and the matter of the altar with everything appertaining to it, of which he as high priest could not be ignorant, but he was a timeserver who sought to curry favour with his prince — and when the sacrifices followed as commanded it was like king like priest, both apostates and idolaters. He identifies the brasen altar as the one Solomon made, standing in the court by the door before the Lord at the eastern frontispiece of the temple, and notes that Urijah was not to be commanded by the king in matters of worship but to attend to the laws and institutions of God.

debates.question: Was the king’s interest in the altar artistic or idolatrous?

Idolatrous, as is evident from the parallel, where he sacrificed to the gods of Damascus because they helped the kings of Syria
Both: his fancy was taken by the carving, and he thought it no harm to join in their devotions while there

A use reserved to the king, who might enquire God’s will by sacrifices joined with prayer
A thing about which he would consider
Consulting God, with Rashi; or a thing to think about; or simply something to look at, an ornamental duplicate

positions.view: He prostituted his authority and betrayed his trust, and the plea that he kept the king at the temple does not excuse him

The high priest who appears as the credible witness of the prophecy, his official position securing his credit

outliers.claim: Alone in allowing that the sacrifice may have gone to Jehovah, and alone in noting that every version but the Targum has the king go up upon the altar, making him his own priest as Uzziah had been.
Alone in prosecuting Urijah at length, and alone in setting Naaman’s borrowed earth against Ahaz’s borrowed altar.
Alone in giving the distance to Damascus, Bunting’s hundred and sixty miles.

17.pericope_label: Ahaz mutilates the bases, the laver and the sea, removes the covert for the sabbath and the king’s entry, and dies

schools.summary: Gill explains the furniture: the ten lavers in which the priests washed stood upon bases of brass, about which were borders bearing the figures of various creatures, lions and oxen and cherubim, and these Ahaz cut off either to deface them in contempt or to convert the brass to other uses, as he might the bases themselves once the lavers were removed. On the covert for the sabbath he offers three possibilities — for the people to sit under while the law was explained by the priests, or for the course of priests going out that day while the entering course had not yet departed, or rather for the king himself while attending the service of that day — and inclines to the last, suggesting it may have been the cover of the royal scaffold and of rich cloth of gold, taken away for the king of Assyria or to signify that he should not frequent the place any more. On the burial he notes that it was not in the sepulchres of the kings of Israel, as David and Solomon were buried, he being such a wicked prince; and he observes of the closing formula that some of his acts stand in the canonical book of Chronicles and were probably in the annals of the kings of Judah, now lost.

Keil and Delitzsch list the mutilations without conjecture: he broke off the panels of the Solomonian stands, which were ornamented with artistic carving, removed every single basin from them, took the brazen sea from the brazen oxen on which it stood and placed it upon a pedestal made of stones — not, they insist, the stone pavement of the court — and they state plainly that the reason why, or the object with which, Ahaz mutilated these sacred vessels is not given. They take the covered sabbath-stand for a covered place, stand or hall in the court of the temple for the king’s use when he visited on the sabbath or feast-days, and the outer entrance of the king for the special royal ascent mentioned earlier, allowing that in what the removal consisted it is impossible to determine for want of information about its original character; and they reject as quite arbitrary the view of Ewald and Thenius that the phrase means he robbed these places of their ornaments in the house of Jehovah. Ellicott calls the covert a very obscure expression and settles for the covered hall or stand set apart for the king and his attendants when he visited the temple on holy days, a reading attested by the Vulgate and by the Syriac’s house of the sabbath, noting that the thing is mentioned nowhere else and that in the house means within the sacred precincts, probably the inner forecourt, while the king’s entry without is the gate by which he entered the inner court. He offers as an alternative rendering the very sense Keil and Delitzsch dismiss, that Ahaz altered these places in the house of the Lord, that is, stripped them of their ornamental work; and he presses the preposition, reading not for the king of Assyria but from fear of him, since Ahaz durst not appear before Tiglath without a present, and allowing that he may also have anticipated a visit from the great king.

Henry reads the whole as Ahaz abusing the temple, not the building but its furniture. The bases and the molten sea were what the priests used for washing, so against them he seems to have had a particular spite, and it is one of the greatest prejudices that can be done to religion to obstruct the purifying of the Lord’s ministers. The covert he takes to have been erected either in honour of the sabbath or for the convenience of the priests when they officiated in greater numbers, and in removing it Ahaz intended to put a contempt upon the sabbath and so to open as wide an inlet as any to all manner of impiety. The king’s entry, perhaps the very ascent which Solomon had made and the queen of Sheba admired, he turned another way to show that he did not intend to frequent the house of the Lord any more, and this he did for the king of Assyria, who perhaps returned his visit and found fault with the entry as an inconvenience and a disparagement to his palace — whence Henry’s moral, that when those who have had a ready passage to the house of the Lord turn it another way to please their neighbours, they are going down the hill apace towards their ruin. He closes on the succession: Ahaz resigned his life in the midst of his days at thirty-six and left his kingdom to a better man, Hezekiah proving as much a friend to the temple as his father had been an enemy; and perhaps this was the very son he had made to pass through the fire and so dedicated to Moloch, but God by his grace snatched him as a brand out of the burning.

Wesley says outright that the form and use of the covert are now unknown, and reports it generally understood of some building — where the priests whose weekly course had ended abode until the next course came, the change being made on the sabbath; or where the guard of the temple kept their station; or that under which the king used to sit to hear God’s word and see the sacrifices, called the covert of the sabbath because the chief times he used it so were the weekly sabbath and the other solemn days of feasting or fasting, which all come under the name of sabbaths, on which the king more solemnly presented himself before the Lord; and he takes the entry for the way by which the king went from his palace to the temple. Clarke notes a great number of conjectures about the word, which with others from the same root signifies covering or booths, and allows either a canopy erected on sabbath days for the accommodation of the people, which Ahaz took away to discourage them from that worship, or a canopy under which the king and his family reposed, transported elsewhere to accommodate the king of Assyria on a visit; he adds the supposition of Jarchi that it was a sort of covert way the kings of Judah had to the temple, removed lest the Assyrian going by it and seeing the sacred vessels should covet them and ask them of a man in no condition to refuse, so that the removal cut off the communication between the king’s house and the temple and left the one passage to which the priests alone had access. On the burial he reads the exclusion from the royal sepulchres as undoubtedly intended for a mark of degradation, and closes with a verdict: the reign was disastrous because it was impious, a scourge and not a blessing, polluting all the cities of Judah with idolatry, so that no worse king had yet sat upon that throne — and this though he had for counsellor one of the greatest men ever produced in the nation and God condescended to interpose for him against two kings who were cut off according to the prophet’s prediction. He would not lay it to heart, and so the wrath of God fell heavily upon him and upon the stiff-necked people he governed: he had sufficient warning and was without excuse, he would sin, and therefore he must suffer.

debates.question: What was the covert for the sabbath?

positions.view: Its form and use are now unknown; three buildings are commonly proposed — for the outgoing priests, the temple guard, or the king
A covered hall or stand set apart for the king and his attendants on holy days, as the Vulgate and Syriac attest
Most likely the cover of the royal scaffold, perhaps of rich cloth of gold
A canopy for the people, or for the king, or, with Jarchi, a covert way to the temple removed lest the Assyrian covet the vessels

debates.question: What was done to the covert and the entry, and why?

positions.view: They were removed; the reading that he merely stripped them of their ornaments is quite arbitrary
Offers that very reading as an alternative, and takes the phrase as from fear of the king of Assyria rather than for him
Done to put contempt on the sabbath and to show he would not frequent the house of the Lord any more, obliging an Assyrian who found fault with the entry
The removal cut the communication between palace and temple so the Assyrian should not enter by the priests’ passage

debates.question: Why were the sacred vessels mutilated?

positions.view: The reason is not given
Either to deface them in contempt or to convert the brass to other uses
A particular spite against the vessels the priests washed in, obstructing the purifying of the ministry

outliers.claim: Alone in relaying Jarchi’s covert way, removed lest the Assyrian see the sacred vessels and covet them, and alone in closing with a formal verdict on the whole reign.
Alone in reading the succession back into the fire of chapter’s opening, Hezekiah snatched as a brand out of the burning from the dedication his father had made of him.
Alone in reading the preposition as from fear of the king of Assyria rather than for him.

themes: king Ahaz cut off the borders of the bases, and removed the laver from off them
took down the sea from off the brasen oxen that were under it
put it upon a pavement of stones
the covert for the sabbath that they had built in the house
the king’s entry without, turned he from the house of the LORD
the rest of his acts which he did, are they not written in the book of the chronicles
Ahaz slept with his fathers, and was buried with his fathers in the city of David
Hezekiah his son reigned in his stead
